title: Does uniform randomized circuit learning imply P equals NP?
formal: Does the existence of a uniform randomized polynomial-time learner for arbitrary Boolean circuits under the uniform input distribution, with membership queries and the resource bounds below, imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\)?

source_formulation.text: However, while some progress on the opposite implications has been made, they remain open, cf. \([2, 33]\).
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 2

why: Asks whether the difficulty of predicting efficiently computable functions follows from worst-case NP hardness alone. The question probes the gap between worst-case complexity, learning and the average-case hardness used in cryptography; its significance depends on keeping their models and quantifiers distinct.
status_note: This is a user-authorized uniform randomized specialization of the source’s broader efficient-learning converse. The checked source and saved later-work review do not resolve it. Reviewed on 13 September 2026; the exact resource specialization is editorial and the inaccessible journal text is not claimed to have been checked.

progress.text: The conference introduction records the circuit-learning-to-P-equals-NP converse as open; it does not fix all of the uniformity conventions selected here.
The later paper studies hardness with agnostic, representation and output restrictions, which must be distinguished from this learning model.

sentences: The premise asks for one efficient learner for all Boolean circuits when it may make membership queries.
Accuracy is measured on uniformly random Boolean inputs, and the output may be any suitably small Boolean circuit.
The learner is uniform and randomized, with explicit polynomial dependence on target size, error and confidence.
The chosen conclusion is the deterministic class equality P equals NP.
This fixes the uniformity choices in the source’s broader converse question without treating randomized or nonuniform conclusions as equivalent.

definitions: Targets are Boolean functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) computed by finite acyclic fan-in-two AND/OR and unary NOT circuits with constants and one output. The target description explicitly lists gates and wire indices; its binary length is at most a supplied bound \(s\). A single oracle Turing machine \(A\) receives \(1^n,1^s\) and binary rationals \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1/2\), and may query \(f(x)\) at any chosen \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Queries may be adaptive and cost the time to write the query plus one step for the answer. The learner has independent fair random coins and no advice, target description or additional oracle. It outputs an explicit deterministic Boolean circuit \(H\) over the same basis. For every permitted input and target it must satisfy \(\Pr_{A\text{ coins}}[2^{-n}|\{x:H(x)\ne f(x)\}|\le\varepsilon]\ge1-\delta\). There is one fixed polynomial \(p\) bounding its time, queries and output length on every random tape by \(p(n+s+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\lceil\log_2(1/\delta)\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon)+\operatorname{len}(\delta))\). The hypothesis need not lie within the target’s size bound; its encoding must obey this output bound. The quantifiers range over every \(n,s\ge1\) and every function with a target description of size at most \(s\). P is the class of languages decided by uniform deterministic polynomial-time Turing machines. NP consists of languages with polynomial-length witnesses checked by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier. Equality concerns languages on all binary inputs, not promise classes. The conclusion is deterministic P equals NP even though the learner is randomized. The implication allows arbitrary proofs and use of the fixed learner code; it is not restricted to black-box reductions.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of this exact implication, or a Lean refutation proving the learning premise together with P different from NP. A proof only of NP containment in BPP or a nonuniform circuit inclusion would not establish the displayed deterministic conclusion. Proper-learning, agnostic-learning or restricted-reduction hardness alone does not refute the premise.

context_blocks.text: The source asks whether efficient circuit learning is equivalent to P equals NP, and separately asks about the absence of strong pseudorandomness. This card addresses the first converse only.

The user-authorized completion selects a single uniform randomized learner with polynomial dependence on target size and the stated accuracy and confidence parameters. It keeps the source’s P equals NP conclusion, without identifying it with a randomized or nonuniform inclusion.
The 2025 follow-up concerns different learning and representation restrictions; its result is not a blanket hardness theorem for the unrestricted improper learner specified here.
